note: Outside the stated ICP on all three commercial criteria, and inside it on both physical ones — which is exactly the pattern that makes the stated definition look mis-specified. Misses successful: a pickleball coach, formerly a tennis coach, currently doing a few private lessons a week; not a business owner, physician or equivalent. Misses income: no meaningful income during treatment, and savings actively being consumed by privately funded oncology as an Australian non-resident — 'everything's coming out of my savings.' Misses neglected_health, decisively and in the opposite direction from the usual failure: the criterion asks for health as the neglected area rather than a crisis, and this is an unambiguous crisis — an aggressive brain cancer eight weeks post-surgery, mid-radiotherapy, with a year of chemotherapy ahead. Matches good_to_great in the narrow fitness sense the criterion tests: he is explicit that he is not seeking rescue — 'definitely not like get lift heavy weights or get extremely stronger, I just want to like build a bit of core, a bit of mobility.' Matches not_deconditioned emphatically: plays roughly 12 hours of pickleball across a weekend, strength trains three times a week, swings a 25 kg kettlebell. The finding worth escalating is that the stated ICP has no clinical criterion at all, so a prospect in active cancer treatment can pass two of its five tests and be sold six to twelve months of loaded training with nothing in the definition stopping it — the same structural blind spot already noted against the Tyron Giuliani assessment, arriving here in a far more serious form. Judged on the criteria, not the outcome; the call ended in a follow-up, but the rating would be identical had it closed.
